extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journalists, bioethicists and science communicators interested in media coverage of neuroenhancement
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analysis and evaluation of newspaper reporting on the non-medical use of prescription drugs for cognitive enhancement, focusing on how prevalence, evidence, benefits and risks are portrayed. Includes search, inclusion/exclusion, coding taxonomy, and coder-reliability procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence portrayal classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify each media article according to its overall portrayal of the prevalence of neuroenhancement using categories: (1) Neuroenhancement is common, widespread or high in prevalence; (2) Uncommon or low prevalence; (3) Unknown prevalence; (4) Neuroenhancement is increasing in prevalence; (5) No mention of the prevalence. Articles that describe neuroenhancement as both 'common' and 'increasing' are noted as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each category (e.g. 'Both medications are common on college campuses...' = common). Early agreement rate between two independent raters was reported (82%); disagreements were resolved by discussion/consensus. Some articles included a counter view but not strongly enough to change overall impression; such counter views were recorded. Use these categories consistently when coding overall tone about prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence type coding for prevalence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim about prevalence within an article, classify the evidence the article cites as: (1) Anecdotal evidence; (2) Academic research/studies/papers; (3) Scientist or researcher opinion/quotation; (4) Other expert opinion/quotation (e.g. physicians, university representatives); (5) No evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded text segments ranged from sentences to whole paragraphs; multiple claims per article are possible and should each be coded. Academic research was later split into 'named academic research/studies/papers' (author or journal explicitly named) and 'unspecified research/studies/papers' (generic references to 'studies' or 'research' without citation). Provide examples when available (e.g. quotes of participants = anecdote; citation of Maher (Nature) = named academic source).

rubrics_metrics.name: Named vs unspecified academic source distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between claims that cite 'named academic research/studies/papers' (explicitly naming authors or journals) and those that cite 'unspecified research/studies/papers' (generic references to 'studies' or 'research' without identifying details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code named sources separately (e.g. Maher (2008), Sahakian & Morein-Zamir (2007), Greely et al. (2008)). The paper notes that unspecified references often over-extend or misinterpret underlying findings; recording this distinction helps identify misrepresentation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits coding taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Code each article for the possible benefits of prescription drugs for neuroenhancement mentioned. Categories include: general improve brain/mental function (non-specific), improve concentration, better exam/academic performance or better grades, improve memory, stay awake/reduce fatigue, increase alertness, help study, improve attention, work faster/more productive, relieve jet-lag, increase intelligence, enhance learning, increase motivation, 'better than caffeine', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code both claims that drugs produce benefits and self-reported/possible benefits. Text that implies or asserts efficacy should be coded the same as direct claims. Aggregate counts of articles mentioning each benefit were used in analysis. Note cases where articles express doubt about efficacy (coded separately under 'efficacy uncertain').

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks/side-effects coding taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Code each article for risks or side-effects of neuroenhancement mentioned. Categories include: unspecified risks/side-effects (non-specific dangers), mental health problems (e.g. anxiety, depression), addiction/dependency, heart or blood pressure problems, insomnia, headache, abuse, loss of appetite/nausea, fatality, 'little is known about the risks', etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record both specific and non-specific risk mentions; also tally articles that mention no risks. Aggregate counts were reported (e.g. 58% of articles mentioned at least one risk). Examples and illustrative quotes are provided in the text; use them to calibrate coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and exclusion criteria for article selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Include print newspaper articles that directly discuss the non-medical use of prescription drugs for neuroenhancement (defined as improving cognitive function in those without a disorder). Exclude articles focusing on therapeutic use (e.g. ADHD treatment), enhancement in sport, cosmetic surgery, natural remedies, drug misuse not for enhancement purposes, articles under 50 words, book reviews. Reprinted shorter and longer versions were both considered distinct and included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample restricted to English-language, Factiva-listed newspapers between 1 Jan 2008 and 31 Dec 2010. Use pre-established inclusion/exclusion rules consistently; when in doubt, have independent reviewers compare decisions and resolve via consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy for comprehensive article retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an iterative, comprehensive keyword search (building on prior studies) to capture media reporting on neuroenhancement. The final search string included terms such as: neuroenhance* OR neuro-enhance* OR nootropic* OR cosmetic neurology OR cosmetic psychopharmacology OR (Ritalin OR methylphenidate OR modafinil OR Adderall OR dexamphetamine) AND (enhance OR enhancement OR enhancer* OR enhancing OR cognition-enhancing OR cognitive-enhanc*) OR (memory-boost* OR professional’s pill OR professor’s little helper OR smart fix OR smarts in a bottle OR smart drugs OR brain doping OR brave new brain OR clever pills OR iq-profin) AND (enhance OR enhancement OR ... ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: to capture both academic and popular terminology used in media. Acknowledge that broad terminology may still miss some articles (false negatives). Document the final search terms and database (Factiva) used for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding unit and multiple-claim handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Code each portion of text that describes prevalence (or benefits/risks) as a discrete unit; coded text can range from individual sentences to entire paragraphs. Articles can make multiple separate claims and each claim must be coded independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative analysis software (the study used NVivo 9) to mark and code text segments. This allows counting multiple claims per article and avoids collapsing distinct assertions into a single code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-coder reliability and consensus procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use at least two independent coders to classify items; report initial agreement rates and resolve disagreements by discussion to consensus. In this study, two researchers independently classified prevalence (initial agreement 82%); remaining items were discussed and consensus reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the initial inter-rater agreement, the process used to resolve discrepancies (meeting, discussion), and the software/tools used (NVivo 9). Maintain transparency about who coded what and how disagreements were settled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report prevalence timeframes and precise definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting prevalence statistics, specify the timeframe (e.g. past year, past month, lifetime) and ensure the definition of neuroenhancement is clear (exclude therapeutic use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights misreporting that arises when media present 'lifetime use' or outlier college rates as general prevalence. Always contextualize prevalence estimates with sample scope and timeframe (e.g. McCabe et al.'s 25% was an outlier campus; median past-year prevalence across many colleges was ~3%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish primary research from commentaries and polls
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate primary empirical research (surveys, representative studies) from commentary pieces, expert essays, and informal polls when using them as evidence for prevalence or efficacy claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commentaries by Greely et al., Sahakian & Morein-Zamir, and the Nature online poll (Maher) were often cited as evidence but are not primary, representative prevalence studies. Report limitations of non-representative polls (self-selected samples) and avoid extrapolating their results to broader populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on anecdote or sensationalist language
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present anecdotal reports as proof of widespread prevalence; avoid sensationalist descriptors (e.g. 'brain steroids', 'smart pills') that may normalize or glamorize use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study shows that anecdote-only claims and sensationalist framing can exaggerate perceived prevalence and encourage imitation. Journalists should contextualize anecdotes with empirical evidence and avoid language that could implicitly endorse use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite high-quality primary evidence and give balanced discussion of benefits vs risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should cite well-conducted primary research (e.g. representative surveys) as the basis for prevalence claims and should present benefits and risks with balanced coverage, not emphasizing benefits while downplaying risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper urges reporters to 'cite high quality evidence (i.e. well conducted primary research studies)' and to avoid overstating benefits in ways that may encourage use. Where evidence for efficacy is weak or uncertain, explicitly state that uncertainty (the paper found only 15% of articles questioned efficacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt media guidelines on responsible drug reporting to neuroenhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use or adapt existing media guidelines for drug reporting (e.g. Australian Press Council Guideline No.246(ii)) to minimize unintended encouragement of prescription drug use for enhancement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines limiting details about quantity, methods of administration, and composition (used for illicit drugs) could be adapted for prescription neuroenhancers. The paper suggests reporters avoid giving actionable details that could facilitate access or misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researchers' and editors' ethical obligation to avoid hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers and journal editors should present findings in ways least amenable to misrepresentation and not contribute to inflated claims about prevalence or efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that misleading media accounts sometimes originate with researchers' optimistic extrapolations of preliminary data; thus academics have an ethical duty to include qualifications and avoid overstating implications. Editors should ensure press materials and published pieces include necessary context to prevent hype.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat reprinted article variants as separate records
rubrics_metrics.description: When an article is reprinted in shorter and longer forms, treat both versions as distinct and include them separately in the sample and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study explicitly included both reprinted shorter and longer versions as separate items. This affects counts and may reflect different emphases or omissions between versions; document and analyze such differences where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate and report frequencies of coded items
rubrics_metrics.description: After coding, aggregate counts of articles mentioning each prevalence portrayal, evidence type, benefit, and risk, and report percentages (noting that percentages may not sum to 100% because multiple codes per article are allowed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents aggregated tables (e.g. percent of articles mentioning each benefit or risk). When reporting, clarify denominators (e.g. n=142) and note that articles can have multiple codes so percentages are non-cumulative.
